power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Strategies such as retrieval practice, spaced repetition, and elaboration can strongly influence how efficiently learners acquire and retain knowledge and skills.
However, students often underuse the most effective strategies, perceiving them as ineffective or overly timeconsuming to implement.
Instructors can nonetheless shape students' strategy use through explicit recommendations and course design.
Accordingly, we surveyed 599 Norwegian higher education instructors regarding which strategies they (1) believe are effective, (2) recommend to students, and (3) facilitate through course design.
We also examined whether mandatory university pedagogy training was associated with more evidence-consistent responses.
Overall, instructors ranked elaboration as most effective, while retrieval practice and spaced repetition received considerably lower rankings.
Vignette judgments suggested most instructors believe open-book summarizing is superior to retrieval practice, even at a 7-day retention interval.
Group work was the most frequently recommended strategy, although recommendations rarely made retrieval or spacing demands explicit.
Facilitation practices oriented toward explaining and elaborating were considerably more common than those involving retrieval or spacing.
University pedagogy training showed little association with evidence-consistent beliefs or practices.
Our findings suggest that instructors favor elaborative encoding and undervalue repeated retrieval practice.
Faculty development programs may benefit by moving toward a more mechanism-oriented understanding of learning.
A cornerstone of any education is the development of students' knowledge and skills.

Because nearly all educational programs are time-bound, instructional time must often be used in ways that efficiently develop learners' comprehension, long-term retention, and ability to transfer learning across contexts.

This is especially evident in professional education programs that prepare students for high-stakes practice (e.g., health care, aviation, engineering), where inadequate learning may have substantial practical consequences.
For example, nursing students receive three years of training, only half of which is formal on-campus instruction (European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2005 , 2013).
text.formatted: For example, nursing students receive three years of training, only half of which is formal on-campus instruction <ref type="bibr">(European Parliament & Council of the European Union, 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Within this constrained timeframe, students must acquire complex and safety-critical skills, such as calculating drug dosages, where even minor errors can have serious consequences for patients' health (Stolic et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Within this constrained timeframe, students must acquire complex and safety-critical skills, such as calculating drug dosages, where even minor errors can have serious consequences for patients' health <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Stolic et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This raises a central question for educational practice: which learning and instructional strategies are most efficient for developing knowledge and skills that are both retained over the long-term and transferable across contexts?
In recent decades, memory and learning researchers have made substantial progress in addressing this question.

Using both laboratory experiments and studies conducted in representative educational contexts, researchers have identified the underlying mechanisms of effective learning (Yan et al., 2024) and demonstrated how these can be translated into classroom practice (Agarwal et al., 2021; Mawson & Kang, 2025).
text.formatted: Using both laboratory experiments and studies conducted in representative educational contexts, researchers have identified the underlying mechanisms of effective learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Yan et al., 2024)</ref> and demonstrated how these can be translated into classroom practice <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Agarwal et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Mawson & Kang, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: One early effort to synthesize this body of research was an Institute of Education Sciences report on effective instructional strategies (Pashler et al., 2007).
text.formatted: One early effort to synthesize this body of research was an Institute of Education Sciences report on effective instructional strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Pashler et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the prevailing evidence at the time, the authors identified seven strategies with moderate to strong empirical support, including retrieving information from memory, spacing learning over time, and learning from concrete examples.

Some years later, Dunlosky et al. (2013) reviewed ten learning strategies commonly used by students and categorized them into three levels of utility-high (retrieval practice, spaced repetition), moderate (e.g., elaboration), and low (highlighting, rereading, summarizing).
text.formatted: Some years later, <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Dunlosky et al. (2013)</ref> reviewed ten learning strategies commonly used by students and categorized them into three levels of utility-high (retrieval practice, spaced repetition), moderate (e.g., elaboration), and low (highlighting, rereading, summarizing).

text.text: These classifications were based on the extent to which strategies promote comprehension, long-term retention, and transfer, as well as their generalizability across materials, learner characteristics, and educational contexts.

More recently, the conclusions from both of these early reviews have been supported by subsequent and more targeted systematic reviews and meta-analyses (e.g., Agarwal et al., 2021; Carpenter et al., 2022).
text.formatted: More recently, the conclusions from both of these early reviews have been supported by subsequent and more targeted systematic reviews and meta-analyses (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Agarwal et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Carpenter et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, this body of research indicates that a core set of strategies (e.g., spaced repetition, retrieval practice, elaboration, concrete examples) are consistently identified as most effective and efficient, both when implemented by instructors to support students' learning and when employed by students themselves.
The practical significance of these strategies is evident in numerous applied studies.

As an example, Breckwoldt et al. (2016) compared two versions of an undergraduate emergency medicine course in which identical content was delivered either over 4.5 days (spaced) or 3.0 days (crammed).
text.formatted: As an example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Breckwoldt et al. (2016)</ref> compared two versions of an undergraduate emergency medicine course in which identical content was delivered either over 4.5 days (spaced) or 3.0 days (crammed).

text.text: Students in the spaced condition performed moderately better on procedural knowledge and clinical decision-making (Cohen's d = 0.56).
Importantly, this was achieved without increasing total instructional time, illustrating how small changes in instructional design can improve learning efficiency for important skills.
While many interventions focus directly on helping students understand and use effective strategies, instructors play a crucial role because they shape the learning environment.
Through course design and explicit recommendations, they can influence students' default behaviors and steer them towards more efficient strategies (Masui et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Through course design and explicit recommendations, they can influence students' default behaviors and steer them towards more efficient strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Masui et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Wang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, instructors' experience and knowledge about teaching and learning vary widely, which may influence what they believe to be effective, recommend to students, and facilitate in their courses.

Because university pedagogy training has recently become mandatory for Norwegian faculty (Ministry of Education and Research, 2018), the Norwegian context provides an opportunity to examine how such training relates to instructors' beliefs about learning strategies, and to their recommendation and facilitation practices.
text.formatted: Because university pedagogy training has recently become mandatory for Norwegian faculty (Ministry of <ref type="bibr">Education and Research, 2018)</ref>, the Norwegian context provides an opportunity to examine how such training relates to instructors' beliefs about learning strategies, and to their recommendation and facilitation practices.

text.text: Notably, the national guidelines for university pedagogy training specify that instructors should be able to "choose, justify, and develop appropriate learning activities and assessment methods" [authors' translation] (Universitets-og høgskolerådet, 2022), but these guidelines are formulated at a general level and do not reference specific evidence-based learning mechanisms.

Several previous studies have investigated pre-service and in-service teachers' and instructors' knowledge and beliefs about learning strategies (e.g., Firth, 2021; Granström et al., 2023; Halamish, 2018; Morehead et al., 2016; Surma et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Several previous studies have investigated pre-service and in-service teachers' and instructors' knowledge and beliefs about learning strategies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Firth, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Granström et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Halamish, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Morehead et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Surma et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Many of these studies assess accuracy by asking participants to judge the effectiveness of different strategies in hypothetical learning scenarios.

Findings generally show that instructors perform somewhat better than students in recognizing empirically supported strategies such as retrieval practice and spaced repetition (Morehead et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Findings generally show that instructors perform somewhat better than students in recognizing empirically supported strategies such as retrieval practice and spaced repetition <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Morehead et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, their judgments remain far from fully accurate.

Instructors often struggle with less intuitive strategies such as interleaving (Halamish, 2018), and misconceptions are common-particularly when teachers are asked to explain or justify their evaluations (Granström et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Instructors often struggle with less intuitive strategies such as interleaving <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Halamish, 2018)</ref>, and misconceptions are common-particularly when teachers are asked to explain or justify their evaluations <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Granström et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, when teachers are asked open-ended questions about learning strategies, empirically supported strategies are often mentioned infrequently or not at all (Surma et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Moreover, when teachers are asked open-ended questions about learning strategies, empirically supported strategies are often mentioned infrequently or not at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Surma et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While this line of research offers useful insights into teachers' theoretical understanding of learning strategies, and to some extent that of instructors, it provides limited evidence about how such knowledge translates into pedagogical practice.

Even when instructors endorse empirically supported strategies, they often appear to lack a clear understanding of how these strategies operate or how they can be implemented effectively in instructional settings (Firth, 2018; Granström et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Even when instructors endorse empirically supported strategies, they often appear to lack a clear understanding of how these strategies operate or how they can be implemented effectively in instructional settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Firth, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Granström et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Critically, few studies have examined whether higher education instructors actively recommend these strategies to students or deliberately facilitate their use through course design.
To our knowledge, no prior study has simultaneously examined instructors' beliefs, recommendations, and instructional practices, nor their association with formal pedagogical training.

Addressing this gap is important because overestimating the effectiveness of low-utility strategies-or failing to incorporate high-utility strategies into instruction-may lead to less efficient learning conditions for students.

In the present study, we extend prior work on instructors' knowledge of learning strategies by investigating (1) which strategies instructors believe are effective (via a forcedranking task and mechanism-focused vignettes), (2) which strategies they explicitly recommend to students (via an open-ended question), and (3) which strategies they most often facilitate students' use of within a specific self-selected course.
This design allows us to assess both how well-established strategies are understood and whether they are translated into classroom practice in higher education.

To examine beliefs in greater depth, the vignettes were specifically designed to probe instructors' sensitivity to three core mechanisms of effective learning: spacing, retrieval, and interleaving (Yan et al., 2024).
text.formatted: To examine beliefs in greater depth, the vignettes were specifically designed to probe instructors' sensitivity to three core mechanisms of effective learning: spacing, retrieval, and interleaving <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Yan et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The scenarios test, for example, whether instructors' judgments about strategy effectiveness shift appropriately when the retention interval increases, and whether "active" restudy in the form of writing a summary with an open book is distinguished from retrieval-based learning.

Given that university pedagogy training is now a formal requirement for Norwegian faculty (Ministry of Education and Research, 2018), we also examine (4) whether participation in such training is associated with instructors' beliefs, recommendations, and facilitation practices.

Taken together, this study examines how instructors' conceptions of effective learning relate to their recommendations and course design, and addresses the following research questions: • RQ1: What are instructors' beliefs about the relative effectiveness of various learning strategies, and to what extent do these align with the current empirical evidence?
• RQ2: Which learning strategies do instructors most frequently recommend to their students?
• RQ3: To what extent do instructors facilitate the use of various learning strategies through their course design and teaching practices?
• RQ4: Does participation in university pedagogy courses relate to the degree of instructors' alignment with evidence-based practices across beliefs, recommendations, and facilitation?

Vignettes.

Inspired by previous vignette studies (i.e., McCabe, 2011; Morehead et al., 2016), we developed five short vignettes that focused on three cognitive processes that are recognized as central to effective learning: interleaving, spacing, and retrieval (Weinstein et al., 2018; Yan et al., 2024).

text.text: Each vignette described two groups (Group A and Group B) studying the same material for the same amount of time but using different strategies.

Instructors were asked to predict which group would perform better on a later test using a 5-point scale (1 = "Very likely B",2 = "Somewhat likely B",3 = "Likely equal",4 = "Somewhat likely A",5 = "Very likely A").
The full vignette texts are provided in the supplementary materials (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/A8QXB).

text.text: Interleaving.

The first vignette contrasted interleaving (mixing examples or categories during practice) versus blocking (practicing one category at a time) in a scenario involving classification of different cell types.

As prior research strongly supports the benefits of interleaving in this context (Chen et al., 2021; Firth et al., 2021; Ge et al., 2021), we coded responses as either consistent (favoring interleaving) or inconsistent (neutral or favoring blocking) with evidence-based expectations.
text.formatted: As prior research strongly supports the benefits of interleaving in this context <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chen et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Firth et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Ge et al., 2021)</ref>, we coded responses as either consistent (favoring interleaving) or inconsistent (neutral or favoring blocking) with evidence-based expectations.

text.text: To assess beliefs about the spacing effect, we constructed two matched vignettes.
In both vignettes, one group distributed their practice across ten days (spacing) while the other group concentrated the same practice in two consecutive days (crammed).
Crucially, however, one vignette described a final test 10 days after the last study session (long delay), while the other placed the test just 1 day later (short delay).
This design served two purposes.
First, it allowed us to examine whether instructors generally believed spacing to be more effective than cramming.
Second, it enabled us to assess whether instructors' judgments shifted toward more strongly favoring spacing when the retention interval was longer.

This distinction matters because, although spacing typically enhances long-term learning outcomes, it may offer no advantage-or even a disadvantage-when tests follow soon after learning (e.g., Latimier et al., 2021; Rohrer & Taylor, 2006; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015).
text.formatted: This distinction matters because, although spacing typically enhances long-term learning outcomes, it may offer no advantage-or even a disadvantage-when tests follow soon after learning (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Latimier et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Rohrer & Taylor, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: We designed the vignette pair with this in mind because we anticipated that many instructors held generally negative views of cramming, which could lead them to favor spacing regardless of delay.
However, a broad "cramming is bad" belief does not constitute evidence of conceptions consistent with the spacing effect.
We therefore treated the shift in judgments from the short-to long-delay vignette as the more diagnostic indicator, rather than overall endorsement of spacing.
Given mixed empirical findings at short delays, we did not specify an empirical expectation for the short-delay vignette.
For the long-delay vignette, we treated spacing-favoring responses as evidence-consistent, and responses favoring cramming or judging both strategies equally effective as inconsistent.
Retrieval.

To examine instructors' beliefs about retrieval practice, we developed two vignettes: one contrasting retrieval with passive restudy (rereading), and the other contrasting retrieval with active restudy (open-book summarizing).
Because it was made explicit that the summarizing group had access to the materials while summarizing, retrieval was the only condition that necessarily required recall from memory.

Prior evidence indicates that retrieval is typically superior to both rereading and summarizing for comprehension, retention, and transfer outcomes (e.g., Dobson & Linderholm, 2015; Karpicke & Blunt, 2011; Lechuga et al., 2015; O'Day & Karpicke, 2021).

text.text: We therefore treated retrieval-favoring judgments as evidence-consistent in both vignettes.

However, a recent meta-analysis by Gonçalves et al. (2025) compared elaborative encoding activities (including summarizing) with retrieval practice and found that retrieval does not consistently outperform elaborative encoding activities when retention intervals are short (< 6 days), feedback is absent for the retrieval group, or the task is cued rather than free recall.

(2025)</ref> compared elaborative encoding activities (including summarizing) with retrieval practice and found that retrieval does not consistently outperform elaborative encoding activities when retention intervals are short (< 6 days), feedback is absent for the retrieval group, or the task is cued rather than free recall.

text.text: Our vignettes involved free recall and a seven-day retention interval but did not specify whether students could consult the text afterwards.
To be conservative, we therefore also treated equal performance in the retrieval-versus-summarization vignette as empirically expected.

Instructors' recommendations were assessed with two items.
First, instructors were asked: "Do you recommend specific learning strategies/study techniques to your students?
(Choose all that apply)."

Response options included "No, I do not recommend any…" and "Yes," followed by one or more contexts in which recommendations were provided (i.e., "in class", "during supervision or conversations with students", "by sharing resources in our learning management systems (LMS)", and "other [please specify]").
A follow-up openended item then asked instructors to describe which learning strategies or study techniques they most often recommend.
A total of 378 instructors (63.1%) responded.
Open-ended responses were analyzed using quantitative content analysis, suited for categorizing and quantifying textual data (Krippendorff, 2019; Züll, 2016).

Responses were assigned multiple codes when they contained more than one distinct recommendation (e.g., "Mindmap, read the curriculum both before and after the lectures, collaborate" [authors' translation] was coded as mind mapping, read before/after class, and group work).
Percentages reported in the results reflect the proportion of respondents who mentioned each category at least once.
Notably, 32 responses (8.5%) contained advice that did not fit any recognizable strategy (e.g., "Use Vygotsky Zones") and were classified as uncodable.
To anchor responses in a consistent context, instructors were told to answer all facilitation questions with a single, specific course in mind.
We expected the relevance of strategies to vary by course characteristics-especially exam type and course level.

We therefore collected several characteristics of the selected courses, including level (e.g., first year, PhD-level), final assessment format (e.g., in-person versus take-home exams), and whether the course was mainly practical (e.g., laboratory practice).

Instructors then rated, on a 5-point scale (1 = Very little/Not at all,5 = Very much), the extent to which they structured the selected course to facilitate students' use of specific learning strategies.
Our list included nine strategies based on prior research synthesis (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Pashler et al., 2007), with modifications intended to support more valid interpretation of responses.

This item was worded as "Compile excerpts of texts from the syllabus into a summary."
We included this lower-generativity form specifically to provide a contrast with more effortful strategies in the facilitation set.

text.text: Missing data were minimal for the facilitation section (1-9 nonresponses per item) and highest for the ranking task.
Of the 441 respondents who answered at least one item in the final block, 37 (8.4%) skipped the ranking task.
The remaining 404 all provided complete rankings.
Given the low level of missingness, we analyzed available cases without imputing data.

We analyzed the ranking task and retrieval vignette pairs using a Plackett-Luce model (Luce, 1959; Plackett, 1975), implemented with the PlackettLuce package (Turner et al., 2025; Turner et al., 2020).

text.text: This approach is well suited to ranking data because responses are interdependent within respondents, such that placing one strategy higher necessarily constrains the ranks available to the others.
For paired comparisons in the retrieval vignettes, the model reduces to a Bradley-Terry-type model (Bradley & Terry, 1952), with an extension that accommodates ties (Turner et al., 2020).

text.text: Worth estimates were scaled to sum to 1 and can be interpreted as the model-implied probability that a strategy would be ranked first (ranking task) or selected as more effective (paired comparisons), based on the set of compared strategies.

text.text: To facilitate sub-group comparisons for RQ4, we also computed an evidence consistency index from the vignette responses.
Scores were -1 (evidence-inconsistent), 0 (neutral/equal), or +1 (evidence-consistent).

For the retrieval versus open-book summarizing vignette, responses favoring retrieval or indicating equal performance were scored as evidence-consistent (+1), whereas favoring open-book summarizing was scored as evidenceinconsistent (-1).
The short-delay spacing vignette was not scored for evidence-consistency due to mixed empirical expectations.

Instead, a spacing-sensitivity score captured whether respondents shifted their judgment toward spacing (+1), showed no categorical shift (0), or shifted toward cramming (-1) when the retention interval increased from short to long delay.
The overall evidence-consistency index was computed as the mean of the five vignette scores (range -1 to +1), with higher values indicating greater alignment with empirical expectations.
Instructors' effectiveness rankings showed a clear hierarchy (Table 3).
text.formatted: Instructors' effectiveness rankings showed a clear hierarchy (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">3</ref>).

text.text: Elaboration was rated most effective by a wide margin.
Summarizing and retrieval practice formed a second tier with comparable ranks, followed by spaced repetition.
Highlighting, crammed repetition, and repeated rereading were consistently ranked least effective and received minimal worth.
Table 4 summarizes instructors' judgments across the five vignette comparisons.

text.text: For the interleaving vignette, most instructors made judgments that were not evidenceconsistent, with only a minority favoring interleaving.
Instructors generally expected the spacing group to outperform the cramming group in both vignettes.
This judgment pattern was evidence-consistent for the long-delay vignette, but for the short-delay vignette, where empirical expectations are less clear, responses still tended to favor spacing.
It should also be noted that about 10% of instructors favored cramming in the long-delay vignette, which strongly deviates from empirical expectations.
Additionally, as detailed in the analysis section, we computed an evidence-consistency index ranging from -1 to +1.
Scores were modestly positive on average (n = 435; M = 0.160, SD = 0.356; median = 0.200; range = -0.800 to 1.000).
To assess whether instructors were sensitive to the retention interval, we analyzed the shift in judgments from the short-delay to the long-delay vignette.

On average, responses shifted modestly toward spacing (mean shift = 0.46, SD = 1.29), and an ordinal mixed-effects model with a fixed effect of delay and a random intercept for instructor confirmed this shift (OR = 2.43, 95% CI [1.86, 3.18], p < .001).

text.text: The average masked considerable heterogeneity.
Across the full sample, 40% of instructors shifted toward spacing, 43% showed no change, and 17% shifted in the opposite direction.
The no-change group partly reflects a ceiling effect, because 63 of its 181 instructors (35%) had already selected the most pro-spacing option at the short delay and could not shift further.
Among instructors whose short-delay response left room to move (n = 330), 51% shifted toward spacing, 36% showed no change, and 13% shifted toward cramming.
Notably, 19% of instructors never expected the spaced group to outperform the crammed group at either delay.
We categorized instructors' responses to characterize different response profiles based on the two retrieval vignettes (Table 5).
text.formatted: We categorized instructors' responses to characterize different response profiles based on the two retrieval vignettes (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_3">5</ref>).

text.text: The most common profile favored open-book summarizing over retrieval, while also favoring retrieval over rereading.
A smaller group favored retrieval over both rereading and summarizing, which is the pattern most consistent with empirical expectations given the vignette conditions.
Notably, about 13% of instructors responded either opposite to empirical expectations (i.e., did not favor retrieval in either vignette) or judged all strategies to produce equal outcomes.

A sensitivity test using a stricter preference threshold (absolute deviations ≥ 2, with deviations of 1 treated as partial preferences rather than ties) increased the proportion classified as mixed or partial to 74%, indicating that strong and consistent differentiations across the two vignettes were less common.
The Plackett-Luce model worth estimates converged with the simpler rule-based categorization.
Summarizing was estimated to have a worth of 76.3% [71.8, 80.5], followed by retrieval at 22.3% [18.3, 26.6] and rereading at 1.4% [0.9, 2.0].
Brackets denote 95% bootstrapped CIs.
It should however be noted that because summarizing and rereading were not directly compared, their relative ordering is inferred indirectly via their comparisons with retrieval.
Most instructors (78%) reported recommending learning strategies to students, whereas 22% reported that they did not.
Recommendations were most commonly provided during teaching (56%) and/or in supervision or individual conversations (43%), while 32% also reported sharing resources in the learning management system.
The open-ended responses typically contained multiple recommendations (M = 2.04, Mdn = 2, range = 0-9).

A subset of the open-ended responses (5.8%) was coded as "other" because they were more generally oriented, such as recommending students to listen to podcasts about a topic or instructors explaining that they shared links to learning strategy resources.
Among the open-ended recommendations (n = 378), the most frequently mentioned strategies were group work (39.2%) and completing practice assignments or coursework (20.4%).
Using concrete examples or studying cases was recommended by 14%, often framed as a way to connect theory and practice.

Teaching or explaining to others was also somewhat common (13%), as were recommendations to read or review the provided course materials (12.4%) and to specifically prepare by reading before and/or after class (11.9%).
General recommendations to just practice a lot (e.g., "practice, practice, practice") were mentioned by 9.3%.

Explicit recommendations to use retrieval practice (e.g., self-testing, practice exams) were less common (7.9%), and spaced repetition (1.6%), flashcards (1.6%), and studying worked examples (0.5%) were rare.

text.text: Responses to the facilitation questions were anchored to a single course that each instructor supervised and/or taught.

Most respondents selected a course for which they were both course coordinator and instructor (71%), while 25% selected a course they taught at least three hours in without course-coordinator responsibility.
Of the selected courses, 22% were described as mainly practical.
The courses were most commonly second-or thirdyear (40%), followed by first-year (25%) and fourth-or fifth-year courses (21%).
Fewer respondents referenced sixth-year (3%) or PhD-level courses (2%), and 8% indicated "other" level.
The final assessment format (exam type) was most commonly an in-person, supervised school exam (48%), followed by an unsupervised take-home exam (31%).
Around 13% reported using a mixed format (in-person + take-home exams) and 8% selected "other [specify]" and described formats such as artistic performances.
As shown in Figure 1, instructors most strongly facilitated activities such as using concrete examples and cases, preparing for class, and elaboration through why/how questions.

text.text: Facilitation of revisiting concepts over time (spaced repetition) and activities involving explaining or teaching to others were also relatively common.
In contrast, instructors less often reported facilitating the use of worked examples, and strategies that more directly emphasize retrieval demands, such as retrieval practice and pretesting.
For compilation-style summarizing, a small minority of instructors reported high facilitation (13% endorsing 4-5).

To reduce the dimensionality of the facilitation items and limit multiple comparisons, we conducted an exploratory factor analysis using complete cases (n = 568) with the psych package in R (Revelle, 2026).

Using minimum residual (minres) extraction with oblimin rotation (polychoric correlations), we compared 2-4 factor solutions and retained a two-factor model.

This solution was the most coherent (≥ 3 salient loadings per factor, minimal cross-loadings), had the lowest BIC (-88.6), and showed acceptable fit (RMSEA = .069, 90% CI [.057, .083]; TLI = .84; RMSR = .045).

Factor 1, labeled the Explain-Elaborate composite, showed its highest loadings on explaining/teaching others (.70), elaboration (.66), pre-class preparation (.55), organizing/structuring (.46), and use of concrete examples/cases (.44), with a smaller loading for specifying learning goals (.36).

Factor 2, labeled the Retrieval-Spacing composite, showed the highest loadings on retrieval practice (.67), pretesting (.49), and worked examples (.43), with a smaller loading for spaced repetition (.30).
The compilation-style summarizing item did not reach the salience threshold on either factor (.28 and .18) and had low communality (h² = .141).
To summarize instructors' facilitation, we computed two composite indices by averaging the items loading on each factor (1-5 scale; higher scores indicate more facilitation).

Facilitation was higher for the Explain-Elaborate composite (M = 3.34) than for the Retrieval-Spacing composite (M = 2.88), t(596) = 13.00, p < .001, mean difference = 0.46, 95% CI [0.39, 0.53], Cohen's dz = 0.53.

For the Retrieval-Spacing composite, exam type was not significantly associated with facilitation, F(3, 579) = 2.53, p = .056, ηp² = .013, whereas course level was, although the effect was small, F(5, 579) = 3.98, p = .001, ηp² = .033.

Post hoc comparisons indicated higher Retrieval-Spacing facilitation in first-year courses (ΔM = 0.301, 95% CI [0.127, 0.486], p = .020) and second-or third-year courses (ΔM = 0.294, 95% CI [0.122, 0.463], p = .009) than in fourth-and fifth-year courses.

First, we tested the association between university pedagogy course status (UniPed status) and the evidence-consistency index derived from the vignette scores.
A one-way ANOVA indicated that the groups did not differ, F(4, 429) = 0.52, p = .724, ηp² = .005.
This conclusion did not change when teaching experience was added as a covariate.
Next, we tested whether instructors' strategy rankings differed based on UniPed status.
As the UniPed status group "signed up but not started" was very small (n = 9 in the ranking sample), it was excluded from subgroup comparisons.

We compared the rankings using pairwise likelihood-ratio tests on the worth estimates from the Plackett-Luce model (i.e., the model-implied probability that a strategy would be ranked first given the set of alternatives).
For each pair of UniPed groups, we contrasted a model in which the two groups shared a common worth profile with a model that allowed group-specific worth profiles.
P values were Holm-adjusted across the pairwise tests.
Only one pair differed reliably; the "completed < 5 years ago" versus "completed > 5 years ago" groups, χ²(6) = 26.81, p < .001.
text.formatted: Only one pair differed reliably; the "completed < 5 years ago" versus "completed > 5 years ago" groups, χ²(6) = 26.81, p < .001.

text.text: Both groups placed elaboration first.
The primary difference between these two groups was the relative placement of summarizing and retrieval practice.

Instructors who completed pedagogy training < 5 years ago ranked retrieval practice second (worth = 17.6%) and summarizing third (worth = 14.4%), whereas those who completed training > 5 years ago ranked summarizing second (worth = 21.4%) and retrieval practice third (worth = 15.8%).

text.text: The remaining strategies followed the same ordering in both groups with highlighting, crammed repetition, and repeated rereading ranked lowest.
We then examined whether UniPed status was related to the facilitation composites derived from the EFA.
For the Explain-Elaborate composite, facilitation differed by UniPed status, F(4, 590) = 3.04, p = .017, ηp² = .020.
Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons indicated higher scores among instructors currently attending UniPed compared with those reporting no UniPed (mean difference = 0.29, p = .044).
For the Retrieval-Spacing composite, facilitation also differed by UniPed status, F(4, 590) = 2.63, p = .033, ηp² = .018.

Post-hoc comparisons indicated slightly higher scores among instructors who had completed UniPed within the past five years compared with those who have not taken the course (mean difference = 0.23, p = .037).
Finally, we examined whether learning strategy recommendations differed by UniPed status.
We excluded recommendation types with very low prevalence (< 5%) to reduce unstable comparisons, leaving 16 of 26 recommendation types for analysis.

text.text: Because recommendations were coded as binary (present vs. not present), we conducted Pearson chi-square tests for each recommendation type.
To account for multiple testing, we used a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of .003 (α = .05/16).
No test met this threshold (smallest p = .18), indicating no evidence of differences in recommendation types based on UniPed status in our sample.

We surveyed higher education instructors about their beliefs, recommendations, and facilitation of various learning and instructional strategies, and whether university pedagogy training (UniPed) was associated with more evidence-consistent responses.
Overall, our findings paint a complex picture which suggests that instructors' beliefs and practices are partly consistent and partly inconsistent with current empirical understandings.

For instance, instructors correctly assigned low ranks to repeated rereading and highlighting but they ranked elaboration well above retrieval practice and spaced repetition, and ranked summarizing similarly to retrieval practice.
A parallel pattern emerged for facilitation.

Instructors often reported facilitating beneficial strategies such as concrete examples and elaboration, but much less frequently facilitated the use of retrieval practice, pretesting, and worked examples, all of which have strong empirical support.
Finally, UniPed status showed no association with instructors' evidence-consistency.
Regarding strategy effectiveness beliefs (RQ1), the vignette responses provided the most fine-grained insight into instructors' understanding of the mechanisms underlying effective learning.

Most instructors did not recognize the advantage of interleaving over blocking, consistent with previous work identifying interleaving as one of the least understood evidence-based strategies (Halamish, 2018; Morehead et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Most instructors did not recognize the advantage of interleaving over blocking, consistent with previous work identifying interleaving as one of the least understood evidence-based strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Halamish, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Morehead et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: For retrieval practice, the dominant response profile (57%) favored retrieval over rereading but simultaneously judged open-book summarizing as superior to retrieval, and only 19% of instructors consistently favored retrieval across both comparisons.

Because summarizing with open materials reduces the need to recall from memory, this pattern suggests that many instructors view effective learning as primarily dependent on elaborative encoding of study materials, without fully recognizing that retrieving information from memory is a particularly potent learning mechanism.
For spacing, instructors generally favored spaced over crammed practice, but a substantial minority did not adjust their judgments to the retention interval.
Among instructors whose short-delay response left room for change, 51% shifted toward spacing at the longer interval, while 36% did not change and 13% shifted toward cramming.
In addition, 19% never expected the spaced group to outperform the crammed group at either delay.

This pattern suggests that many instructors may not fully consider how spacing interacts with retention intervals when evaluating learning strategies, which could influence how courses and assessments are designed.

Taken together, the moderate evidence-consistency across vignettes suggests that many instructors do not clearly distinguish between strategies that improve short-term performance and those that more reliably support durable and transferable learning (Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015).
text.formatted: Taken together, the moderate evidence-consistency across vignettes suggests that many instructors do not clearly distinguish between strategies that improve short-term performance and those that more reliably support durable and transferable learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Instructors' recommendations (RQ2) largely mirrored the pattern observed in their beliefs.

Although most instructors (78%) reported recommending learning strategies to students, these strategies were not necessarily those with the strongest empirical support, a pattern consistent with findings that such strategies are rarely mentioned by teachers (Surma et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although most instructors (78%) reported recommending learning strategies to students, these strategies were not necessarily those with the strongest empirical support, a pattern consistent with findings that such strategies are rarely mentioned by teachers <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Surma et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Group work was the most frequently recommended strategy.
One possible explanation is that instructors value its social and motivational benefits, which are well documented and important (Kroeper et al., 2025; Zengilowski et al., 2023).
text.formatted: One possible explanation is that instructors value its social and motivational benefits, which are well documented and important <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Kroeper et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Zengilowski et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, the extent to which group work benefits students' learning depends heavily on how it is implemented (e.g., Mende et al., 2021; Song et al., 2025), and may be conditional on students' working memory capacity and prior knowledge (Andrews & Rapp, 2015; Hood et al., 2023).
text.formatted: However, the extent to which group work benefits students' learning depends heavily on how it is implemented (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Mende et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Song et al., 2025)</ref>, and may be conditional on students' working memory capacity and prior knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andrews & Rapp, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Hood et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, non-contingent recommendations to work in groups are unlikely to produce reliable learning benefits.
Notably, explicit recommendations to use retrieval practice were much less common, and spaced repetition was seldom mentioned.

Some frequently recommended activitiessuch as completing practice assignments-may implicitly involve retrieval, but the low frequency of explicit mention suggests that instructors do not consistently frame these activities in ways that make the underlying learning mechanisms apparent.

This may be consequential because students already misinterpret the mental effort associated with effective strategies as a sign of poor learning (Kirk-Johnson et al., 2019) and perceive more passive and fluent instruction as more effective, even when it is not (Deslauriers et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This may be consequential because students already misinterpret the mental effort associated with effective strategies as a sign of poor learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Kirk-Johnson et al., 2019)</ref> and perceive more passive and fluent instruction as more effective, even when it is not <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Deslauriers et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: It is also well documented that mental effort is generally aversive (David et al., 2024), suggesting that people will gravitate towards lower-effort strategies unless they understand the necessity or value of engaging in a more effortful activity.

text.text: Without explicit framing from instructors, students may complete practice assignments in ways that reduce retrieval demands-for instance, by relying on open-book resources or AI tools rather than attempting recall from memory (Blasiman et al., 2017; Pan et al., 2025).

text.text: Recent national data indicate that 72% of Norwegian students sometimes or often use AI tools to study, most commonly for explanations or summaries of course material (Norwegian Directorate for Higher Education and Skills, 2026).
While this may support elaborative encoding, it does not require retrieval or facilitate spaced repetition.

Given that students may be particularly receptive to concrete strategy recommendations from their instructors (Carpenter & Sanchez, 2025), this represents a missed opportunity to shape students' self-regulated learning.
text.formatted: Given that students may be particularly receptive to concrete strategy recommendations from their instructors <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Carpenter & Sanchez, 2025)</ref>, this represents a missed opportunity to shape students' self-regulated learning.

text.text: Instructors' facilitation practices (RQ3) clustered into two broad dimensions: an Explain-Elaborate composite and a Retrieval-Spacing composite, with the former being facilitated considerably more often than the latter.
Although this pattern may partly reflect how the items were formulated, at least two additional, non-mutually exclusive interpretations should be considered.
First, instructors may recognize the value of repeated retrieval but regard it primarily as the students' responsibility.

From this interpretation, instructors focus on explaining the material and supporting students' understanding, whereas practicing and retaining that knowledge is implicitly left to students' independent study.

Second, and perhaps more consistent with the vignette findings, instructors may not fully appreciate the value of repeated retrieval because they assume that elaborative encoding-through activities such as summarizing, elaboration, or group discussion-is sufficient to produce durable learning.
This assumption is not unreasonable.
Elaborative and generative activities do support learning, and can complement retrieval practice (McDaniel, 2023).

text.text: Such activities may even outperform retrieval practice under some conditions (Fiorella, 2023; Gonçalves et al., 2025), and it is well established that making material meaningful and linking new information to prior knowledge improves comprehension and subsequent memory (Bransford & Johnson, 1972; van Kesteren et al., 2018).

text.text: However, although more elaborative encoding can improve both immediate and delayed performance, emerging evidence suggests that it raises the level of initial learning without substantially reducing the rate at which information is subsequently forgotten (Peng et al., 2025; Rivera-Lares et al., 2022).

text.text: If so, the practical implication is that even wellunderstood material remains vulnerable to forgetting over typical educational time intervals.

Moreover, knowledge and skills that appear well established when assessed within a few days may show substantial additional forgetting across longer intervals (Radvansky et al., 2022), and the fluent performance produced by elaborative activities in the short term can easily be misread as evidence of durable learning (Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015).

text.text: If instructors assume that strong initial understanding is largely sufficient for long-term retention, they may systematically underestimate how much students forget-even after high-quality instruction.
This underestimation may itself have a cognitive basis.

Research on metacognition suggests that people are often poor at anticipating their own forgetting. Koriat et al. (2004) found that individuals who had recently studied material expected to remember it nearly as well after a week as after a day, and Kornell and Bjork (2009) found that learners substantially underestimated how much additional practice would improve later retention.

text.text: If a similar stability illusion applies to instructors, it could help explain why elaborations, explanations, and concrete examples are facilitated more often than repeated retrieval, despite substantial evidence that repeated retrieval practice is more efficient.
Lastly, our results indicate only a few minor associations between UniPed status and more evidence-consistent responses (RQ4).

Instructors who completed UniPed less than five years ago assigned slightly higher worth estimates to retrieval practice and slightly lower estimates to summarizing, but only relative to those who completed the course more than five years ago.
There were no differences in instructors' recommendations.

For facilitation, those currently attending UniPed scored slightly higher on the Explain-Elaborate composite and those who completed UniPed less than five years ago scored slightly higher on the Retrieval-Spacing composite, although both effects were small.

These largely null results suggest that university pedagogy courses at the two institutions we investigated have not substantially shaped instructors' understanding of central learning mechanisms, or at least not sufficiently to be detected with a cross-sectional survey of this kind.
This likely reflects the content and emphasis of past courses rather than the potential of such programs.
The clearest practical implication of our findings relates to faculty development, perhaps most immediately through university pedagogy courses.

While there have been significant efforts in recent years to promote active learning in higher education, our findings suggest that instructors are not adequately familiar with the mechanisms that make a learning activity more or less effective.

Specifically, instructors promote activities such as elaboration, summarizing, and group discussion, which may be seen as active, without recognizing that their effectiveness ultimately depends on whether they engage core mechanisms underlying effective learning, such as retrieval from memory.

Faculty development and university pedagogy programs could therefore benefit from moving beyond broad dichotomies such as active versus passive or deep versus surface, towards a mechanism-oriented understanding grounded in the cognitive processes that underlie effective acquisition, retention, and transfer of learning.
Moreover, across nearly all measures, a small but meaningful minority of instructors (approximately 10-30%) responded in ways that were opposite to evidence-based expectations.

This suggests that faculty development efforts need to reach not only the majority who may benefit from a more nuanced understanding, but also instructors whose current conceptions may actively undermine effective instruction.
Retrieval and spacing stand out as two particularly important target mechanisms.
Most instructors in our study correctly recognized retrieval practice as superior to rereading, which is encouraging.
Many also recommended doing practice assignments.
However, the majority did not make retrieval demands explicit, and favored open-book summarizing over retrieval practice.
If instructors gain a more accurate understanding of when and how retrieval practice supports learning, they may design and recommend activities that better support durable and transferable learning.
Regarding spacing, it is important that instructors understand how the timing and distribution of repetitions affects short-term performance versus long-term retention and transfer.
This is clear in professional education, where teaching is sometimes organized in intensive blocks.
In nursing programs, for instance, high failure rates on drug dosage calculation exams have been a persistent challenge (Alteren & Nerdal, 2015; McMullan et al., 2010).

text.text: From a memory perspective, this is problematic.

Crammed practice can reduce immediate failure rates and produce confident learners even though it can compromise long-term retention and students' ability to transfer what they have learnt (Rohrer, 2015; Soderstrom & Bjork, 2015).

text.text: Studies also indicate that learners can become "grossly overconfident" after crammed practice compared with spaced practice (Emeny et al., 2021; Kornell & Bjork, 2007; Logan et al., 2012), meaning that instructors who optimize for short-term outcomes may foster learners that are both overconfident and underprepared.

text.text: A central strength of this study is that we examined instructors' understanding and application of learning strategies across three related but distinct measures: beliefs about strategy effectiveness, open-ended recommendations to students, and self-reported facilitation of strategies in teaching.

Additionally, to better distinguish evidence-consistent from evidence-inconsistent implementations (e.g., "reading the same text multiple times in a row"), we took particular care to formulate items that captured meaningful differences in how strategies were implemented.
This was motivated by studies demonstrating that item wording can substantially affect conclusions.

For example, Malain and Hartwig (2026) showed that previously observed null associations between self-reported spaced study and academic performance were likely driven by how "spaced study" had been operationalized.

text.text: However, the important limitation that follows is that our questionnaire has not been previously validated.

Although validated instruments exist for assessing both students' learning strategies (Pintrich et al., 1993) and instructors' teaching activities (Williams et al., 2015), these did not offer the precision needed to distinguish between effective and ineffective implementations.

text.text: Our approach therefore trades established psychometric properties for increased conceptual precision.
Furthermore, self-report measures do not necessarily reflect real-world behavior (Podsakoff et al., 2003).

text.text: This concern may be particularly relevant for the facilitation items.

For instance, although rigorous implementations of spaced repetition appear uncommon (Rohrer, 2015), instructors in our sample reported facilitating spacing relatively often, which could reflect minimal practices such as mentioning last week's content, or including an end-of-semester recap lecture rather than more systematic implementations.

text.text: Finally, our sample was drawn from only two institutions, with the majority of respondents from one university.

The observed associations-or lack thereof-between university pedagogy training and instructors' beliefs and practices therefore reflect the characteristics of these specific courses, and not university pedagogy courses in general.
Future research should address these limitations in at least two ways.
First, the survey items developed here could be subjected to systematic validation work, including assessment of reliability across different contexts and languages.
Second, self-report measures could be complemented with more behavior-proximal indicators, such as analysis of course materials and assignments or structured observation of classroom practices.

Regarding the vignettes specifically, future versions should include a rereading-versussummarizing comparison, specify the presence or absence of feedback for retrieval practice, and clarify that the final test format includes both factual recall and comprehension, so that instructors do not vary their responses based on assumptions about what the test measures.
We examined how higher education instructors understand, recommend, and facilitate various learning strategies.
To their credit, instructors correctly identified lowutility strategies such as rereading and highlighting, and most recognized that retrieval practice is superior to restudy.
However, instructors less often supported strategies such as interleaving, pretesting, spaced repetition, and worked examples, and the majority favored open-book summarizing over retrieval practice.
Retrieval and spacing were also rarely mentioned in recommendations, and elaboration-oriented activities were facilitated considerably more than retrieval-based practices.
University pedagogy training showed little association with more evidence-consistent beliefs or practices.

Together, these findings suggest that many instructors hold an incomplete understanding of the mechanisms that support durable and transferable learning-emphasizing elaborative encoding and undervaluing repeated retrieval practice.

Bridging this gap will require faculty development that moves beyond abstractions such as active versus passive learning toward a more mechanism-oriented understanding of how effective learning works.
